ob.plans.title: Plans take longer than we think
ob.plans.detail: Most people guess too low. A good list shows the real shape of your day.
ob.plans.caption: Time to finish a senior thesis, on average.
fact.loops: Unfinished goals kept popping into people’s heads. Making a specific plan stopped those intrusions.
fact.loops.src: Source: J. of Personality and Social Psychology, 2011
fact.pings: In one study, interrupted people worked faster but felt more stress, frustration and time pressure.
fact.plans: Students expected 33.9 days to finish a thesis. It took 55.5. Only 29.7% finished when predicted.
fact.plans.src: Source: J. of Personality and Social Psychology, 1994
fact.name: Setting a phone reminder is “cognitive offloading”: your device carries part of the mental load.
fact.role: Right after switching tasks, people respond more slowly and usually make more mistakes.
fact.struggle: A review of 691 correlations found that unpleasant and far-off tasks strongly predict putting things off.
fact.areas: Over 12 weeks, unfinished work on Friday was linked to worse weekend sleep through brooding.
fact.areas.src: Source: J. of Occupational Health Psychology, 2017
fact.peak: Time of day affects attention and memory, and it depends on whether you lean morning or evening.
fact.day: People who wrote a to-do list before bed fell asleep faster than those who listed finished tasks.
fact.day.src: Source: J. of Experimental Psychology: General, 2018
fact.capacity: Detailed plans help with one goal, but that boost didn’t carry over to many goals at once.
fact.focus: Short breaks gave a small, real lift in energy and less fatigue across 22 study samples.
fact.capture: In a lab study, speaking a short English message was 2.93 times faster than typing it.
fact.reminders: Just getting a phone notification disrupted focus, even when people never touched the phone.
fact.reminders.src: Source: J. of Experimental Psychology: HPP, 2015
fact.celebrate: Across 128 studies, positive feedback raised interest, while expected tangible rewards lowered it.
fact.first: If-then plans (“when X happens, I’ll do Y”) helped goals across 94 studies and 8,000+ people.
fact.weekly: Across 138 studies, checking progress made goals more likely, even more so when written down.
